blocks.text: Ezekiel 43 opens with the prophet's vision of YHWH's glory returning to the sanctuary, approaching from the east and entering to fill the house completely (vv. 1-5). This moment represents the culmination of a narrative arc that structures the entire book: Ezekiel has previously witnessed the departure of the divine glory from the defiled Jerusalem sanctuary (chapters 8-11), and here he now sees its return to the visionary, measured sanctuary. The text emphasizes the continuity of this experience by explicitly referencing the prophet's earlier encounters—verse 3 compares this vision to the appearance seen "when I came to destroy the city" and to previous visions "by the river Chebar." The sensory imagery—the sound like many waters, the earth shining with the divine glory—conveys the overwhelming presence of YHWH.

Ezekiel 43 is positioned centrally within the prophet's extended vision of chapters 40-48, which presents a comprehensive restoration of the sanctuary and covenant community. This vision encompasses the measured architectural structure of the sanctuary, the returned divine glory (which arrives in chapter 43), the restored altar and priestly service, the proper offerings, and the reestablished relationship between YHWH and the covenant community. The return of the glory in verses 4-5 represents the pivotal moment when the vision is activated: the sanctuary becomes the actual dwelling place of YHWH in the midst of Israel.
